"My husband is no fool—he married me."—A witness at Bow County Court.
A meeting of the Hongkong Board of Education will be held in the Board Room at the Education Office on Wednesday, June 10th at 3 o'clock.

A small army of Paris shop girls are wearing wigs, which they discard on leaving, the premises where they work. Shingled heads have been banned by their directors, under threat of immediate dismissal, and there was nothing left to do but to make the best of a bad job—which the pretty wigs they wear show they have done.

Contests for the Canadian typewriting championships were held simultaneously in five cities of Canada. Miss Irma Wright, of Toronto, won the one-minute contest with a speed of 117 words a minute. This says the "Daily Mail," is far behind the feat of the 29-year-old Miss Millicent Woodward, of Mansfield, England, champion typist of Europe, who, in December, 1922, typed 276 (memorised) words in one minute. She was credited then with receiving £1,000 a year as chief demonstrator for a firm of typewriter manufacturers.
"Because he wanted to see what would happen," he told the magistrate, Victor Reed, aged 17, put three baulks of timber, on a road near Castor, Cambidagshire frequented by motorists. He was fined.

A well-dressed clerk of the Eastern Telegraph Co., delivering cables during the messenger boys' strike went to a London hotel. A porter took his hat and umbrella and showed him into a room. Then a woman came in, exclaiming, "It's so nice of you to have called. Will you come up and see the wedding presents!"
In spite of the fact, a considerable number of farm hands from Great Britain and European countries are being distributed on western Canadian farms, the supply is not equal to the demand and shortage is becoming more pronounced as spring work develops more extensively. Wages are averaging from $30 to $40 (gold) per month and board.

Mr. Tom Johnston, the Socialist M.P. for Dundee, is to ask the Premier whether Government accepts the rule that members of the Cabinet, during their tenure of office, should refrain from contributing articles to the Press upon public affairs and whether he is aware that Lord Birkenhead is a voluminous contributor to newspapers upon matters affecting public policy, and as to what steps, if any, he proposes to take. It may be noted that Lord Birkenhead is at present contributing a series of articles to the "Evening Standard" upon the divorce laws.

One hundred families of Hebridean settlers for the Vermillion district of the Province of Albert were expected to arrive during the latter part of May. In the past three years hundreds of settlers from the Hebrides Islands of Scotland have come to Canada under the auspices of the Scottish Immigrant Aid Society, most of whom have been successfully established in Alberta.

"Oh, sir!" exclaimed the junior reporter of the "Morning Papyrus" (with which the contemporary Munsey had merged the Alexandria "Scarab," retaining the best features of both). "Oh, sir! The asp has bitten Cleopatra!" How many times, growled the grizzled news editor, "have I got to tell you that that isn't news? Now, if Cleopatra had bitten the asp___."

The home-c ming of Lord Reading is deeply saddened for him by the untimely death of Godfrey Isaacs. The affection was particularly strong between these brothers, each so brilliant a leader in his chosen walk of life. Though the elder by six years, and in his way quite as hard a worker as his brother, Lord Reading happens to have been blessed with by far the more versatile mind, and has always understood the art of cultivating varied interests and the necessity for hard brain-workers, of mental recreation. On the other hand, Godfrey Isaacs was always so utterly possessed and obsessed by his job that it was no easy matter to get him to take even a passing interest in anything else. For the last fifteen years the Maronji Company and its affairs had been his life, and what he was forced by the doctor to retire from the ago worn out with overwork and want of rest he had the appearance of a man who had nothing to live.

Since the Duke and Duchess of York returned from East Africa Her Royal Highness has been kept very busily engaged at her home at White Lodge in arranging the large number of interesting souvenirs of almost every description that they have brought back with them. In due course several of the sporting trophies that fell to the rife of the Duke of York are to be placed in position. White Lodge, with its many windows and light and airy appearance, lends itself admirably to a display of this description. The Duchess of York has also brought home a large collection of specimens of native workmanship, some of which are quite unique of their kind. Some of these are destined as presents for the intimate friends of the Duke and Duchess.

Passengers departing for Home by the S.S. Moreyon Saturday included Mrs. E. B. C. Hornell, Captain and Mrs. P. R. Purslow, Paymaster Commdr. E. T. Green, Mr. and Mrs. W. G. Wheeler, Commdr. L. H. B. Bevan, Mr. C. P. Cavé, Lieut. R. J.

Now celebrating its 100th birthday, the Wesleyan Chapel, St. Germans, Cornwall, owes its origin to a false pair of butcher's scales. By means of the scale a servant to the Earl of St. Germans unjustly accused the butcher of fraud. The Earl, in reparation, offered the man anything he liked to select. He chose a site for a chapel.

A rabbit in flight near Elm Spring, Arkansas, led to the discovery by a shpoting party of a man's skeleton in the hollow of a giant oak (says the "Central News"). When the rabbit took refuge in the hollow, whose opening was only a few inches wide, the "hunters" enlarged the entrance and found the skeleton, also an old flintlock rifle and a buckskin pouch of gunpowder, Foresters judge that it must be over 60 years since the opening was large enough for the man to creep through. Perhaps he took refuge when pursued by Indians. Perhaps he could not so turn as to get out again. Or he may have been wounded and died in the tree, which has since grown up around him. James's Payn's story of the "Lost Sir Massing-berd" is recalled by the discovery.

A marriage-will shortly take place between Cecil Edward Truford, M.C., and Monica, younger daughter of Sir Hugh Clifford, G.C.M.G., Governor-General of Nigeria, and the late Minna Clifford.
Engineer Commander and Mrs. H. B. Sears left on Saturday by the 8.8. Tjikärung for a holiday in Java.
Teachers are wanted for French, Spanish and shorthand classes in Maidstone Prison.

Reuter cables the death of Mr. J. B. Suttor, formerly Far Eastern Commissioner for New South Wales, at Kobe. Mr. Suttor was well-known in Hongkong. He passed through the Colony quite recently on his way back to Japan. During the war he attended an annual meeting of the Hongkong Chamber of Commerce.

Mr. B. A. Hale, editor of the "Daily Press," left by the Moreau on Saturday for a holiday in England. He is returning in October next. Mrs. Hale and their son, Mr. Bertram Hale, who is with Messrs. Thos. Cook and Son at Shanghai, are also spending this summer at Home. Mrs. Hale left by the Porthos about a month ago and Mr. Bertram Hale went from Shanghai via the Panama Canal.

Mr. Henry Arthur Jones, the dramatist, at a Shakespeare celebration alluded to the fact that he was born in a farm house in Buckinghamshire under conditions rather similar to those of Shake. Spears. "I told this fact to my granddaughter the other day," he said, and she replied. "If you were born in the next county but one to Shakespeare, why don't you write better plays?" (Laughter.)

The King's early return from his holiday did not surprise anybody in the Court circle. It was an open secret that His Majesty went abroad most unwillingly, and only upon the urgent representations of his doctors. The effect of the change has entirely justified the medical advice. But the King was anxious to be back for the resassembling of Parliament after the Easter recess. Two couriers a week have kept him in close touch with affairs, but when Parliament is sitting the King likes to be on the spot.

An estimate of the life-work of Sun Yat-sen leads a writer in "Asia" (New York) to compare the three men who, by common consent, are estocried the greatest men of modern Asia. They are Gaudhi, Mustapha Kemal Pasha, and Sun Yat-sen. But between Sun and the other two, he any, there is this unlikeness: Gandhi has the respect, the worship even, of the Indians, and Kemal the power over the Turks; but Sun Yat-sen is regarded by the Chinese with indifference and sometimes with mockery. Yet Sun Yat-sen no less than the other two is entitled to his place in the triumpeate that may truly be said to have fired with new spirit in the aged soul of the East. Indeed he was the first of the three and made the talk of the other two to the other.
Though pressure has been brought upon her by her friends, Lady Astor declares she has no intention of retiring from Parliament.
The engagement is announced of Miss Muriel Stanhope, of Melbourne, Australia, and Seremban, to Mr. L. V. J. Laville, of the Malayan Civil Service.
Mr. Eina V. Schou, the millionaire margarine king, has died in Denmark. In 1889 he began business with one ton of margarine which he invented, and was soon manufacturing 1,000 tons a week.

Mabel Normand, the film actress, has accepted an offer of £500 a week from Mr. Norman Lee, revue producer, connected with the Gulliver circuit. He will present her in a musical play to be produced in Manchester and London in the autumn. A feature will be a film studio scene. Mr. Lee has also engaged Mr. Bryant Washburn, Miss Normand, has not appeared in films lately. Her name was mentioned in connection with a shooting affair nearly two years ago.

A most successful dance, to which the officers of the warships were invited, was given by Sandakan Club in the Club premises on the 13th May. We congratulate the organisers on the excellence of the Arrangements and of the supper. Dances in Sandakan do not unfortunately occur very often, but when they do they go with a fine swing and this one was no exception to the rule, its success being enhanced by the presence of the Carllale's jazz band, which was kindly lent for the occasion.

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that an Extraordinary General Meeting of the above Company will be held at the Registered Office of the Company, Queen's Building, Victoria, Hongkong, on TUESDAY, the 2nd day of June, 1925, at 11 o'clock in the forenoon, when the subjoined Resolutions which were passed as Extraordinary Resolutions at the Extraordinary General Meeting of the Company held on the 18th day of May, 1925, will be proposed for confirmation as Special Resolutions, viz.:

(1) That the Articles of Association of the Company be altered in manner following that is to say by the deletion of Article 17 and by the substitution therefor of the following article, namely:—
“17. So long as the issued “capital of the Company” shall not exceed $6,000,000 “no member shall be entitled to be registered as the “holder of more than 8,000 shares of the Company.” Should the issued capital “of the Company be increased,” “ed beyond $6,000,000,” the “number of shares in respect of which a member shall be entitled to be registered shall be increased,” “proportionately, but no member shall be entitled to be registered in respect of “a fraction of a share.””

(2) That the authorised Capital of the Company (which is now $3,000,000 consisting of 60,000 shares of the nominal value of $50 each the whole of which have been issued) be increased to $10,000,000 by the creation of 140,000 additional shares of the nominal value of $50 each ranking (subject as herein-after mentioned) for dividend and in all other respects pari passu with the shares constituting the Company's present issued Capital.

(3) That 60,000 of the said 140,000 new shares be offered in the first instance (in the proportion of one new share for every old share held by them respectively) to the members of the Company who on the 10th day of June, 1925, are registered in the Company's Share Register as the holders of the said 60,000 old shares at a premium of $10 per share.

(4) That the aforesaid offer be made to members by notice specifying the number of new shares to which a member is entitled. That a member whose registered address is situate in the Far East or his nominee shall pay for such new shares accepted by two instalments, i.e., one instalment of $80 per new share to be paid on or before the 15th day of July, 1925, and a further instalment of $80 per new share to be paid on or before the 15th day of October, 1925, and such member or his nominee who has not accepted and lodged with the Company's Bankers the first instalment due on such new shares on or before the 15th day of July, 1925, will be deemed to have declined. That a member

situate outside the Far East or his nominee shall pay for such new shares accepted by two instalments, i.e., one instalment of $30 per new share to be paid on or before the 15th day of September, 1925, together with interest calculated at the rate of 6 per cent. per annum on the total amount then payable for the period from the 15th day of July, 1925, until the date of receipt of payment by the Company's Bankers and a further instalment of $30 per new share to be paid on or before the 15th day of December, 1925, together with interest calculated at the rate of 6 per cent. per annum on the total amount then payable for the period from the 15th day of October, 1925, until the date of actual receipt of payment by the Company's Bankers and such member outside the Far East or his nominee who has not accepted and lodged with the Company's Bankers the first instalment due on such new shares on or before the 15th day of September, 1925, together with interest as aforesaid will be deemed to have declined. The Directors shall have the right to reject any nominee.

(5) That such of the said 60,000 new shares as shall be accepted by members both in and outside the Far East shall be a-vis the said 60,000 old shares rank for dividend as from the 15th day of July, 1925, to the extent of one half of the nominal value of such new shares and as from the 15th day of October, 1925, equally with the said 60,000 old shares.

(6) That any of the said 60,000 new shares which shall not be taken up by the Company's shareholders in manner aforesaid and the remaining 80,000 unissued new shares may be issued and disposed of in such manner at such time or times and upon such terms as to ranking for dividend and otherwise as the Company's Directors shall in their absolute discretion think fit.

The TRANSFER BOOKS of the Company will be closed from WEDNESDAY, the 10th day of June, 1925, to WEDNESDAY, the 17th day of June, 1925, (both days inclusive) during which period no transfer of shares can be registered.
Dated the 20th day of May, 1925.
By Order of the Board of Directors,
R. M. DYER
